data.question: Your take-home pay is 2,000 GBP a month. Using the 50/30/20 rule, how much should go toward savings and extra debt repayment each month?
data.explanation: The 50/30/20 rule sends 20% to savings and debt. 20% of 2,000 GBP is 400 GBP.

data.question: Your first review shows monthly income of 2,000 GBP and expenses of 2,100 GBP. By how many GBP are you overspending each month?
data.explanation: Expenses (2,100) minus income (2,000) is a 100 GBP monthly shortfall — the gap you need to close first.

data.question: Your monthly expenses are 2,000 GBP and you want a 3-month emergency fund. Saving 300 GBP each month, how many months will it take to reach the goal?
data.explanation: A 3-month fund is 6,000 GBP. At 300 GBP a month, 6,000 / 300 = 20 months.

data.question: You have a 50,000 GBP deposit for a 200,000 GBP property. What is your Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratio, expressed as a percentage?
data.explanation: You borrow 150,000 GBP of the 200,000 GBP price. LTV = 150,000 / 200,000 = 75%.

data.question: A property rents for 1,000 GBP/month. Annual costs are: mortgage 7,200, insurance 600, maintenance 1,200, void allowance 600. What is the annual NET rental income in GBP?
data.explanation: Gross rent is 12,000 GBP/year. Costs total 9,600 GBP. Net = 12,000 - 9,600 = 2,400 GBP.

data.question: You set aside 10% of annual rental income for maintenance. If the property earns 12,000 GBP per year, how many GBP should you set aside?
data.explanation: 10% of 12,000 GBP is 1,200 GBP — a realistic maintenance reserve protects your cash flow.

data.question: A rental earns 1,200 GBP/month. The mortgage is 700, insurance 50, and you set aside 150 for maintenance and vacancies. What is the monthly NET cash flow in GBP?
data.explanation: Costs total 900 GBP. Net cash flow = 1,200 - 900 = 300 GBP per month.

data.question: A liquidity pool charges a 0.3% fee per trade and handles 1,000,000 EUR of trades in a day. What is the total daily fee earned by liquidity providers, in EUR?
data.explanation: 0.3% of 1,000,000 EUR is 3,000 EUR, shared among providers in proportion to their share of the pool.

data.question: Drag these financial goals into the order you should fund them, from first (top) to last.

items.label: Pay off a credit card at 19% APR

data.explanation: Secure a safety net first, then clear high-interest debt (a guaranteed 19% return), then invest for growth, and treat a holiday — a want — last.

data.question: Using the Debt Avalanche method, drag these debts into the order you should pay them off, from first (top) to last.
data.explanation: The Avalanche method always attacks the highest interest rate first, because that debt costs you the most money each month.
